data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The Central Bank of Samoa pegs the tala to a basket of trading-partner currencies, so inflation is largely imported and volatile: a series high of 14.6% in 2009 after the tsunami and global food-price spike, near-zero readings through the mid-2010s, outright deflation of -3% in 2021 during the COVID border closure, then 8.7% in 2022 and 12% in 2023 on the global commodity shock. The IMF projects 1.9% for 2025, back to normal. With the exchange rate doing the stabilizing work, domestic monetary policy is a minor lever; remittances and tourism flows matter more for demand.
debt_management: Debt rose from 33.5% of GDP in 2006 to a series high of 56.4% in 2015, driven by post-2009-tsunami reconstruction and concessional infrastructure borrowing, notably from China. Since then it has been one of the Pacific's cleanest deleveraging stories: steady repayments, solid growth and grant financing brought it down every year to a projected 21.2% in 2025, the series low. The trajectory shows that small island states can work down disaster-driven debt when the borrowing was concessional and growth resumes - though the low base also reflects how little fiscal space Samoa retains for the next shock.

key_events.event: September tsunami killed nearly 200 people and devastated the south coast, driving a debt-funded rebuild.
December: Cyclone Evan caused widespread damage, the second major natural disaster in three years.
December measles epidemic prompted a state of emergency and a mass vaccination campaign.
April election and constitutional crisis ended 22 years of HRPP rule; Fiame Naomi Mata'afa became the first female prime minister.
COVID-19: borders stayed closed until August 2022, shielding health but freezing tourism.

outlook_next_decade: Debt is low and falling, which gives Samoa rare fiscal room among Pacific islands - the question is whether it is used for climate-resilient infrastructure or consumed by current spending. Remittances and tourism underpin the economy; both are hostage to Australian and New Zealand conditions. Political stability after the 2021 crisis held, but coalition fragility is a watchpoint. The base case is steady, unspectacular growth with the next cyclone resetting the fiscal clock.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
